sub: Named after “the clinging clot” (ʿalaq) in ayah 2
theme: It opens with the first words ever revealed, a command to read in Allah’s name. Then it warns the arrogant man who tried to stop the Prophet ﷺ from praying: don’t obey him, prostrate and draw near.
story: Ayat 1–5 were the first revelation. The Prophet ﷺ was worshipping alone in the cave of Ḥirāʾ when the angel came and said, “Read!” He went home trembling, and Khadījah reassured him that Allah would never disgrace him.
She took him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, who said this was the same angel sent to Mūsā, and that his people would one day drive him out.
Ayat 6–19 came later, once the Prophet ﷺ prayed openly at the Kaʿbah. Abū Jahl threatened to step on his neck, and these ayat answered him.

sections.title: First revelation: read, for your Lord created and taught by the pen
sections.meaning: Read in the name of your Lord who created, who made man from a clinging clot. Read, for your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, and taught man what he did not know.
points: Read in the name of your Lord who created
He created man from a clinging clot
Read: your Lord is the Most Generous
He taught by the pen, taught man what he didn’t know
sections.matters: These are the first words of the Quran ever revealed. The first command is to read, tied to Allah’s name, and the first blessings named are creation and knowledge.
sections.story: In the cave of Ḥirāʾ, an angel told the Prophet ﷺ, “Read!” He said, “I am not one who reads.” After pressing him three times, the angel recited these ayat. He went home trembling to Khadījah.
explained: Iqraʾ bismi rabbika: begin reading with your Lord’s name. The unlettered Prophet ﷺ is told that his Lord, who created everything, can make him read. He made man from ʿalaq, a small clinging clot of blood, and the One who shaped man will guide him with a message.

Read again: your Lord is al-akram, the Most Generous. From His generosity He taught writing with the pen, which preserves knowledge, and taught man what he did not know. Man is born knowing nothing; all his knowledge is Allah’s gift.
teaches: Reading and writing are gifts from the Most Generous.
Remember your humble start: a clinging clot.
Whatever you know, Allah taught you.
sections.hook: Iqraʾ opens ayah 1 and ayah 3. Khalaqa comes twice (1–2), then ʿallama twice (4–5): creating, then teaching.

sections.title: Feeling self-sufficient, man oversteps and stops a servant praying; Allah sees
sections.meaning: No! Man oversteps his bounds when he sees himself as needing no one, but the return is to Allah. Look at the one who forbids a servant from praying: what if that servant is guided and urges piety, while the forbidder denies and turns away? Doesn’t he know Allah sees?
points: Man transgresses once he thinks he needs no one
To your Lord is the return
Have you seen the one who forbids a servant who prays?
What if the servant is guided, or commands piety?
What if the forbidder denies? Doesn’t he know Allah sees?
sections.matters: It exposes what wealth and status can do to a proud heart, and its ugliest result: trying to stop someone from praying. The questions make the listener feel how wrong it is, and end with a warning: Allah is watching.
sections.story: Revealed later than ayat 1–5. Abū Jahl swore by al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā to step on the Prophet’s ﷺ neck if he saw him prostrating at the Kaʿbah. When he came near, he backed away in fright.
explained: Kallā: truly, man yaṭghā, crosses the line, once he sees himself as istaghnā, rich and needing no one. While in need he walks straight; once wealthy or powerful he turns arrogant. But to your Lord is the return, and He will ask where the wealth came from and where it went.

Ara-ayta: have you seen anything stranger? A man forbids a servant from praying, when that servant is guided and calls to taqwā, while the forbidder himself denies the truth and turns away. Doesn’t he know that Allah sees what he does, and will repay him?
teaches: Feeling self-sufficient is the start of arrogance.
Wealth and power must be answered for.
Never stand between anyone and their prayer.
Allah sees both the one who prays and the one who blocks.
sections.hook: Ara-ayta, “have you seen?”, opens ayat 9, 11 and 13. The run ends with a different question (14): a lam yaʿlam bi-anna Allāha yarā.

sections.title: Allah will seize his lying forelock; don’t obey, prostrate and draw near
sections.meaning: No! If he doesn’t stop, Allah will seize him by the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock. Let him call his council; Allah will call the angels of Hell. No! Don’t obey him. Prostrate and draw near.
points: If he doesn’t stop, We will seize the lying, sinful forelock
Let him call his council; We will call Hell’s guards
Don’t obey him; prostrate and draw near
sections.matters: The threat and the comfort come together. The bully is helpless before Allah, and the Prophet ﷺ is told what to do: ignore him and keep praying, since prostration is where a servant is closest to his Lord.
sections.story: Reportedly at the Maqām Ibrāhīm, Abū Jahl threatened the Prophet ﷺ and boasted that no one had a bigger gathering in the valley. Ayat 17–18 answered him. Had he called his men, the angels would have seized him.
explained: Kallā: if he does not stop, la-nasfaʿan bin-nāṣiyah: We will grab him by the forelock, the hair over the forehead, and drag him to the Fire. That forelock lies in its words and sins in its deeds. Another view: it will be blackened on Judgement Day.

Let him call his nādī, the men of his council, for help. Allah will call az-zabāniyah, the harsh angels who guard Hell. No! Don’t obey him. Keep praying, prostrate and draw near to Allah; a servant is closest to his Lord in sujūd, so make much duʿāʾ there.
teaches: Don’t obey anyone who stops you from worship.
Crowds and supporters are nothing against Allah.
Sujūd is the closest you get to Allah.
sections.hook: Kallā opens ayat 6, 15 and 19. “Let him call” (fal-yadʿu, 17) is answered by “We will call” (sanadʿu, 18). The last ayah is a place of prostration.

groups.text: Read in the name of your Lord who created, who made man from a clinging clot.
Read, for your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen what man did not know.
Man oversteps when he thinks he needs no one, but the return is to Allah.
Have you seen the man who forbids a servant from praying?
What if that servant is rightly guided, or calls people to taqwā?
What if the forbidder denies and turns away? Doesn’t he know Allah sees?
If he doesn’t stop, Allah will seize his lying, sinful forelock.
Let him call his council; Allah will call the angels who guard Hell.
Don’t obey him. Prostrate and draw near to Allah.

1.explain: Iqraʾ bismi rabbika: read, beginning with your Lord’s name, the One who created everything. The unlettered Prophet ﷺ is told his Lord can make him read.
1.why: The first revelation. In the cave of Ḥirāʾ the angel said “Read!”, and the Prophet ﷺ answered, “I am not one who reads.” The angel pressed him three times, then recited ayat 1–5.

2.explain: He created man min ʿalaq: from clinging clots, the small lump of thick blood the embryo becomes. Such a humble start shows the Creator’s power and care.

3.explain: Iqraʾ again, for emphasis, or now to recite it to others. Wa rabbuka al-akram: your Lord is the Most Generous, patient with people, not rushing to punish.

4.explain: Alladhī ʿallama bil-qalam: He taught writing with the pen, by which knowledge is kept and passed on.

5.explain: He taught man mā lam yaʿlam, what he did not know: guidance, writing and skills. Man is born knowing nothing, so all his knowledge is a gift.

6.explain: Kallā: truly. Yaṭghā: man crosses his limits and grows arrogant toward his Lord.
6.why: Reportedly revealed about Abū Jahl, who, whenever he gained wealth, added to his clothes, his riding animals and his food. Ayat 6–19 came later than ayat 1–5.

7.explain: An raʾāhu istaghnā: because he sees himself as rich and needing no one. While in need he walks straight; once wealthy or powerful, he oversteps.

8.explain: Inna ilā rabbika ar-rujʿā: to your Lord is the return. He will ask where your wealth came from and how you spent it.

9.explain: Ara-ayta: have you seen anything stranger than the one who forbids…
9.why: About Abū Jahl, who swore to step on the Prophet’s ﷺ neck if he saw him prostrating. When he came near, he backed away, saying he saw a trench of fire, terrors and wings.

10.explain: …ʿabdan idhā ṣallā: a servant when he prays, meaning the Prophet ﷺ at the Kaʿbah. He said: had Abū Jahl come near, the angels would have snatched him limb by limb.

11.explain: Have you seen, if the servant he forbids is ʿalā al-hudā, on true guidance, knowing the truth and acting on it?

12.explain: …or commands taqwā, calling others to sincerity and tawḥīd? Is such a person someone to be forbidden?

13.explain: Have you seen, if the forbidder kadhdhaba, denies the truth, and tawallā, turns away from faith?

14.explain: A lam yaʿlam: doesn’t he know that Allah sees him, hears his words and will repay him in full?

15.explain: Kallā: if he doesn’t stop, la-nasfaʿan: We will seize and drag him by an-nāṣiyah, the forelock, into the Fire. Or: blacken it on Judgement Day. Held by the forelock, a person is helpless.

16.explain: Nāṣiyatin kādhibatin khāṭiʾah: a lying, sinning forelock, meaning its owner lies in his words and sins in his deeds.

17.explain: Fal-yadʿu nādiyah: then let him call his nādī, the people of his council and his clan, to help him.
17.why: Reportedly Abū Jahl found the Prophet ﷺ praying at the Maqām and said, “Didn’t I forbid you?” The Prophet ﷺ rebuked him, and he boasted that no one had a bigger gathering in the valley. This ayah answered.

18.explain: Sanadʿu az-zabāniyah: We will call the harsh, stern angels who guard Hell and push its people in. Had he called his men, they would have seized him at once.

19.explain: Kallā, lā tuṭiʿhu: don’t obey him. Wa-sjud wa-qtarib: prostrate and draw near to Allah. A servant is closest to his Lord in prostration. Reciting this ayah calls for a prostration.
